   103                  circumstances as to threaten to impair the national 
   104                  security of the United States. To address the national 
   105                  security threat found in Proclamation 9704, I 
   106                  established a tariff regime, which included imposing ad 
   107                  valorem duties on certain imports of aluminum articles 
   108                  and its derivative articles. In subsequent 
   109                  proclamations, including Proclamation 11021 of April 2, 
   110                  2026 (Strengthening Actions Taken To Adjust Imports of 
   111                  Aluminum, Steel, and Copper Into the United States), 
   112                  and Proclamation 11032 of June 1, 2026 (Further 
   113                  Adjusting the Tariff Regimes for Imports of Aluminum, 
   114                  Steel, and Copper Into the United States), I modified 
   115                  the tariff regime for aluminum to more effectively 
   116                  address the national security threat found in 
   117                  Proclamation 9704.
   118  
   119                  2. In those proclamations, I directed the Secretary of 
   120                  Commerce (Secretary) to monitor the effects of imports 
   121                  of aluminum with respect to the national security, to 
   122                  update me on the status of that threat to the national 
   123                  security, and to provide me with recommendations if 
   124                  circumstances indicated the need for further 
   125                  Presidential action under section 232.
   126  
   127                  3. Based on the Secretary's monitoring, I have received 
   128                  information, opinions, and recommendations from the 
   129                  Secretary regarding the tariff regime imposed in 
   130                  Proclamation 9704, as amended, and the national 
   131                  security threat found in Proclamation 9704.
   132  
   133                  4. Among other things, the Secretary has informed me 
   134                  that the additional ad valorem duties on imports of 
   135                  aluminum are strengthening the American aluminum 
   136                  industries and addressing the national security threat 
   137                  found in Proclamation 9704. In the Secretary's opinion, 
   138                  domestic aluminum production and related domestic 
   139                  aluminum industry would not be as strong as they are if 
   140                  not for the aluminum tariff regime imposed under 
   141                  section 232, and the national security threat found in 
   142                  Proclamation 9704 would be worse than it is if not for 
   143                  the aluminum tariff regime imposed under section 232.
   144  
   145                  5. The Secretary has informed and advised me of his 
   146                  opinion that, despite the benefits from the aluminum 
   147                  tariff regime, the domestic production and supply of 
   148                  primary aluminum, which is critical to the U.S. economy 
   149                  and defense industrial base, is still in insufficient 
   150                  supply. In the Secretary's view, it is important to 
   151                  modify the aluminum tariff regime in a way to more 
   152                  effectively encourage increased domestic production of 
   153                  primary aluminum.
   154  
   155                  6. To ensure that the aluminum tariff regime continues 
   156                  to effectively address the national security threat 
   157                  found in Proclamation 9704, the Secretary recommended 
   158                  that I establish an incentive for companies to engage 
   159                  in building new facilities capable of producing primary 
   160                  aluminum, expanding facilities
   161  
   162  [[Page 46636]]
   163  
   164                  to become capable of producing primary aluminum, or 
   165                  refurbishing outdated facilities that produce primary 
   166                  aluminum to expand their production or increase the 
   167                  efficiency of production. The Secretary recommended 
   168                  that I do this by allowing those companies or their 
   169                  designated representatives to import a quantity of 
   170                  primary aluminum corresponding to the reasonably 
   171                  anticipated annual production of primary aluminum from 
   172                  the new project at a reduced tariff rate. This would 
   173                  build on the program established for certain aluminum 
   174                  and steel from Canada and Mexico in clause 13 of 
   175                  Proclamation 10984 of October 17, 2025 (Adjusting 
   176                  Imports of Medium- and Heavy-Duty Vehicles, Medium- and 
   177                  Heavy-Duty Vehicle Parts, and Buses Into the United 
   178                  States).
   179  
   180                  7. After considering the current information, opinions, 
   181                  and recommendations newly provided by the Secretary; 
   182                  the factors in section 232 (19 U.S.C. 1862(d)); the 
   183                  need to address the national security threat found in 
   184                  Proclamation 9704; and other relevant factors and 
   185                  information, I have determined that it is necessary and 
   186                  appropriate to modify the tariff regime for imports of 
   187                  aluminum imposed in Proclamation 9704, as amended. In 
   188                  particular, I determine that it is necessary and 
   189                  appropriate to establish an investment incentive 
   190                  program for companies investing in new U.S. production 
   191                  capacity for primary aluminum, as further detailed 
   192                  below. In my judgment, the modifications in this 
   193                  proclamation will ensure that the tariff regime imposed 
   194                  on imports of aluminum continue to effectively address 
   195                  the national security threat found in Proclamation 
   196                  9704.
   197  
   198                  8. Section 232 authorizes the President to adjust the 
   199                  imports of an article and its derivatives that are 
   200                  being imported into the United States in such 
   201                  quantities or under such circumstances as to threaten 
   202                  to impair the national security of the United States so 
   203                  that such imports will not threaten to impair the 
   204                  national security.
   205  
   206                  9. Section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (19 
   207                  U.S.C. 2483) (section 604), authorizes the President to 
   208                  embody in the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United 
   209                  States (HTSUS) the substance of statutes affecting 
   210                  import treatment, and actions thereunder, including the 
   211                  removal, modification, continuance, or imposition of 
   212                  any rate of duty or other import restriction.
   213  
   214                  NOW, THEREFORE, I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the 
   215                  United States of America, by the authority vested in me 
   216                  by the Constitution and the laws of the United States, 
   217                  including section 232, section 604, and section 301 of 
   218                  title 3, United States Code, do hereby proclaim as 
   219                  follows:
   220  
   221  (1) The Secretary is authorized to and shall establish a program to 
   222  incentivize new investment in U.S. production facilities to produce primary 
   223  aluminum.
   224  
   225    (a) The Secretary is authorized to solicit and accept onshoring plans 
   226  from companies. Any onshoring plan shall at least include: a commitment, if 
   227  the plan is approved, to build, refurbish, or expand a facility in the 
   228  United States that will produce primary aluminum; a commitment that 
   229  construction will start by January 20, 2029; and any other relevant 
   230  information and analysis, including requirements set by the Secretary.
   231  
   232    (b) The Secretary is authorized to approve onshoring plans described in 
   233  subclause (a) of this clause. In determining whether an onshoring plan 
   234  qualifies for approval, the Secretary, in consultation with any senior 
   235  executive branch officials the Secretary deems appropriate, shall consider 
   236  all relevant factors he deems appropriate, such as the anticipated start 
   237  date of construction, whether the proposed plan's project timeline is 
   238  commercially reasonable, whether the proposed plan's project milestones are 
   239  commercially reasonable, the anticipated annual production of primary 
   240  aluminum from the onshoring project, whether the proposed plan's 
   241  anticipated costs and primary-aluminum production projections are 
   242  reasonable, and how the benefits of the reduced tariff rate will be 
   243  allocated between the applicants of the onshoring plan. When approving 
   244  onshoring plans, the Secretary shall act in a manner consistent with the 
   245  need to address the national security threat found in Proclamation 9704.
   246  
   247  [[Page 46637]]
   248  
   249    (c) If the Secretary approves a company's onshoring plan, the Secretary 
   250  shall allow the company to annually import primary aluminum of a quantity 
   251  that corresponds to the U.S. production facility's reasonably anticipated 
   252  annual output of primary aluminum when the onshoring project is completed, 
   253  at half the section 232 rate of duty otherwise in effect. Tariff 
   254  adjustments awarded for facility refurbishment shall only be granted to the 
   255  extent those adjustments correspond with the value of the company's 
   256  investment.
   257  
   258    (d) The Secretary is authorized to take all actions that he deems 
   259  appropriate to implement and effectuate this program, including, consistent 
   260  with applicable law, the issuance of regulations, rules, guidance, and 
   261  procedures. All approved onshoring plans shall be subject to monitoring and 
   262  enforcement by the Secretary. The Secretary may require that companies with 
   263  approved onshoring plans submit reports to the Department of Commerce to 
   264  ensure compliance with domestic manufacturing commitments, and he may 
   265  require that such reports be audited, including by external auditing firms. 
   266  Should the Secretary determine that a company is substantially failing to 
   267  meet its agreed-upon commitments that are the basis for granting the tariff 
   268  benefits detailed in this proclamation, the Secretary is authorized to 
   269  cease and rescind the tariff benefits awarded pursuant to this 
   270  proclamation. In cases where the executive branch assesses that a company 
   271  engaged in fraud or deliberately misled the United States Government with 
   272  respect to onshoring commitments, the rescission of tariff benefits can be 
   273  retroactive to the extent permitted by law, and the Secretary or the 
   274  Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection may collect the 
   275  additional tariffs owed because of the retroactive rescission of the tariff 
   276  benefits and impose any appropriate fines or penalties to the extent 
   277  consistent with applicable law.
   278  
   279  (2) The Secretary, in consultation with the Secretary of Homeland Security, 
   280  the United States Trade Representative, the Chairman of the United States 
   281  International Trade Commission, and any other senior official the Secretary 
   282  deems appropriate, shall determine whether any modifications to the HTSUS 
   283  are necessary to effectuate or implement this proclamation or any actions 
   284  taken pursuant to this proclamation, and shall make such modifications 
   285  through notice in the Federal Register.
   286  
   287  (3) The Secretary shall continue to monitor imports of aluminum and its 
   288  derivatives. The Secretary shall, from time to time, review the status of 
   289  aluminum and its derivative imports with respect to the national security. 
   290  The Secretary shall inform me of any circumstances that, in his opinion, 
   291  might indicate the need for further Presidential action under section 232. 
   292  The Secretary shall also inform me of any circumstance that, in his 
   293  opinion, might indicate that any of the actions taken under section 232 are 
   294  no longer necessary.
   295  
   296  (4) To the extent consistent with applicable law, the Secretary and the 
   297  Secretary of Homeland Security are directed and authorized to take all 
   298  actions that are appropriate to implement and effectuate this proclamation 
   299  and any actions contemplated by this proclamation--including through

    26  Ending Certain Tariff Actions
    27  
    28                  By the authority vested in me as President by the 
    29                  Constitution and the laws of the United States of 
    30                  America, including the International Emergency Economic 
    31                  Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq.) (IEEPA), the 
    32                  National Emergencies Act (50 U.S.C. 1601 et seq.), 
    33                  section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (19 
    34                  U.S.C. 2483), and section 301 of title 3, United States 
    35                  Code, it is hereby ordered:
    36  
    37                  Section 1. Background. In Executive Order 14193 of 
    38                  February 1, 2025 (Imposing Duties To Address the Flow 
    39                  of Illicit Drugs Across Our Northern Border), as 
    40                  amended; Executive Order 14194 of February 1, 2025 
    41                  (Imposing Duties To Address the Situation at Our

    45                  of China), as amended; Executive Order 14245 of March 
    46                  24, 2025 (Imposing Tariffs on Countries Importing 
    47                  Venezuelan Oil); Executive Order 14257 of April 2, 2025 
    48                  (Regulating Imports With a Reciprocal Tariff To Rectify 
    49                  Trade Practices That Contribute to Large and Persistent 
    50                  Annual United States Goods Trade Deficits), as amended; 
    51                  Executive Order 14323 of July 30, 2025 (Addressing 
    52                  Threats to the United States by the Government of 
    53                  Brazil), as amended; Executive Order 14329 of August 6, 
    54                  2025 (Addressing Threats to the United States by the 
    55                  Government of the Russian Federation), as amended; 
    56                  Executive Order 14380 of January 29, 2026 (Addressing 
    57                  Threats to the United States by the Government of 
    58                  Cuba); and Executive Order 14382 of February 6, 2026 
    59                  (Addressing Threats to the United States by the 
    60                  Government of Iran), I declared or described national 
    61                  emergencies with respect to unusual and extraordinary 
    62                  threats to the national security, foreign policy, or 
    63                  economy of the United States and took actions to deal 
    64                  with those threats, including by imposing, pursuant to 
    65                  IEEPA, additional ad valorem duties on certain imports 
    66                  of certain foreign trading partners.

    68                  In light of recent events, the additional ad valorem 
    69                  duties imposed pursuant to IEEPA in Executive Order 
    70                  14193, as amended; Executive Order 14194, as amended; 
    71                  Executive Order 14195, as amended; Executive Order 
    72                  14245; Executive Order 14257, as amended; Executive 
    73                  Order 14323, as amended; Executive Order 14329, as 
    74                  amended; Executive Order 14380; and Executive Order 
    75                  14382 shall no longer be in effect and, as soon as 
    76                  practicable, shall no longer be collected. All other 
    77                  actions, including any other action taken to address 
    78                  the national emergencies declared or described in 
    79                  Executive Order 14193, Executive Order 14194, Executive 
    80                  Order 14195, Executive Order 14245, Executive Order 
    81                  14257, Executive Order 14323, Executive Order 14329, 
    82                  Executive Order 14380, and Executive Order 14382, that

    87                  emergencies declared or described in Executive Order

    89                  Executive Order 14245, Executive Order 14257, Executive 
    90                  Order 14323, Executive Order 14329, Executive Order 
    91                  14380, and Executive Order 14382 or subsequent orders 
    92                  remain in effect and shall not be affected by this 
    93                  order.
    94  
    95                  Sec. 2. Implementation. (a) To effectuate the 
    96                  terminations of the actions described in section 1 of 
    97                  this order, the head of each executive department and 
    98                  agency (agency) is authorized to and shall take all 
    99                  appropriate steps
   100  
   101  [[Page 9438]]
   102  
   103                  to end the additional ad valorem duties imposed under 
   104                  IEEPA in Executive Order 14193, as amended; Executive 
   105                  Order 14194, as amended; Executive Order 14195, as 
   106                  amended; Executive Order 14245; Executive Order 14257, 
   107                  as amended; Executive Order 14323, as amended; 
   108                  Executive Order 14329, as amended; Executive Order 
   109                  14380; and Executive Order 14382. The head of each 
   110                  agency shall immediately begin taking steps to 
   111                  effectuate this order and, as soon as practicable, 
   112                  terminate the collection of the additional ad valorem 
   113                  duties described in section 1 of this order. The head

   116                  redelegate the authority to take such appropriate steps 
   117                  within the agency.

   119                      (b) The Secretary of Commerce, the Secretary of 
   120                  Homeland Security, and the United States Trade 
   121                  Representative, as appropriate and in consultation with 
   122                  the Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection, 
   123                  the Chair of the United States International Trade 
   124                  Commission, and any other senior official they deem 
   125                  appropriate, shall determine whether modifications to 
   126                  the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States are 
   127                  necessary to effectuate this order and may make such 
   128                  modifications through notice in the Federal Register.
   129                      (c) The Executive Order of February 20, 2026 
   130                  (Continuing the Suspension of Duty-Free De Minimis 
   131                  Treatment for All Countries), and the Proclamation of 
   132                  February 20, 2026 (Imposing a Temporary Import 
   133                  Surcharge to Address Fundamental International Payments 
   134                  Problems), are unaffected by this order.
   135                      (d) This order affects only the additional ad 
   136                  valorem duties imposed under IEEPA pursuant to the 
   137                  Executive Orders described in section 1 of this order. 
   138                  This order does not affect any other duties, including 
   139                  duties imposed under section 232 of the Trade Expansion 
   140                  Act of 1962, as amended, 19 U.S.C. 1862, and section 
   141                  301 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended, 19 U.S.C. 
   142                  2411.

   144                  Sec. 3. General Provisions. (a) Nothing in this order 
   145                  shall be construed to impair or otherwise affect:
   146  
   147  (i) the authority granted by law to an executive department or agency, or 
   148  the head thereof; or
   149  
   150  (ii) the functions of the Director of the Office of Management and Budget 
   151  relating to budgetary, administrative, or legislative proposals.
   152  
   153                      (b) This order shall be implemented consistent with 
   154                  applicable law and subject to the availability of 
   155                  appropriations.

   157  [[Page 9439]]

   163                  entities, its officers, employees, or agents, or any

   160                  goods and services''; has recently reflected quarterly 
   161                  deficits in its return on investment or labor, as 
   162                  reported by the BEA in the ``balance on primary 
   163                  income''; and runs a deficit in voluntary transfers, 
   164                  such as remittances, as reported by the BEA in the 
   165                  ``balance on secondary income.'' In other words, the 
   166                  United States runs a trade deficit, does not currently

   171  
   172                  8. As my advisors have informed me, the United States 
   173                  runs a substantial trade deficit. The large, 
   174                  persistent, and serious annual United States goods 
   175                  trade deficit has grown by over 40 percent in the past 
   176                  5 years alone, reaching $1.2 trillion in 2024. In 2025, 
   177                  the United States goods trade deficit remained at 
   178                  approximately $1.2 trillion. The effects of this 
   179                  deficit are serious, and this deficit contributes to 
   180                  the fundamental international payments problems facing 
   181                  the United States.
   182  
   183                  9. As my advisors have also informed me, the annual 
   184                  balance on the United States primary income turned 
   185                  negative for the first time since at least 1960 in 
   186                  2024. From 1960 to 2023, the United States ran a 
   187                  surplus in its annual balance on primary income. That 
   188                  positive balance on primary income served as a 
   189                  stabilizing force for the United States balance-of-
   190                  payments position even in the face of large and 
   191                  persistent trade deficits. In 2024, however, the 
   192                  balance on primary income turned negative and thus 
   193                  ceased to serve as a counterweight to the trade deficit 
   194                  in the United States current account. Indeed, in 2024, 
   195                  the United States maintained a current account deficit 
   196                  of 4.0 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), almost 
   197                  double the current account deficit of approximately 2.0 
   198                  percent that prevailed between 2013 and 2019, and 
   199                  larger than that which prevailed from 2019 to 2023. As 
   200                  a share of GDP, the staggering deficit of 4.0 percent 
   201                  represented the biggest annual current account deficit 
   202                  since 2008.
   203  
   204                  10. As my advisors have also informed me, the net 
   205                  international-investment position of the United States 
   206                  is in an ongoing decline. According to the BEA, at the 
   207                  end of 2024, the net international-investment position 
   208                  of the United States, as a share of GDP, was negative 
   209                  90 percent, a sharp deterioration from the average of 
   210                  negative 41 percent in the decade between 2010 and 
   211                  2020. In my advisors' view, this is a highly atypical 
   212                  position for a country, particularly the United States. 
   213                  Indeed, both in terms of United States dollars and as a 
   214                  share of GDP, this represents one of the most negative 
   215                  net international-investment positions of any developed 
   216                  country. Because the current account is one of the 
   217                  primary drivers of changes in the net international-
   218                  investment position, the atypically large negative net 
   219                  international-investment position of the United States 
   220                  shows that the United States balance-of-payments 
   221                  deficit is large and serious.
   222  
   223                  11. Further, as my advisors have informed me, the 
   224                  balance on secondary income of the United States has 
   225                  been persistently in a deficit since the 1960s.
   226  
   227                  12. According to my advisors, an import surcharge in 
   228                  the form of ad valorem duties is required to address 
   229                  these fundamental international payments problems. In 
   230                  my advisors' opinions, imposing an import surcharge 
   231                  would deal with the large and serious United States 
   232                  balance-of-payments deficit. My advisors have further 
   233                  recommended that certain products should not be subject 
   234                  to the surcharge because of the needs of the United 
   235                  States economy

   237  [[Page 9341]]
   238  
   239                  and have opined that a surcharge with certain 
   240                  exceptions would more effectively deal with the 
   241                  balance-of-payments deficit than would a surcharge 
   242                  without the exceptions.

   244                  13. After considering the information, opinions, and 
   245                  recommendations that have been provided to me by senior 
   246                  officials, among other relevant information and 
   247                  considerations, I find that fundamental international 
   248                  payments problems within the meaning of section 122 
   249                  exist; that those problems significantly harm United 
   250                  States national interests, including economic and 
   251                  national security interests; and that special measures 
   252                  to restrict imports are required to address those 
   253                  problems, as authorized by section 122. Specifically, I 
   254                  find that a surcharge in the form of ad valorem duties 
   255                  on certain imports is required to deal with the United 
   256                  States' large and serious balance-of-payments deficit. 
   257                  Accordingly, I impose, for a period of 150 days, a 
   258                  temporary import surcharge of 10 percent ad valorem, as 
   259                  described below, on articles imported into the United 
   260                  States, effective February 24, 2026.

   298                  restrictions imposed pursuant to section 232 of the 
   299                  Trade Expansion Act of 1962, as amended (19 U.S.C. 
   300                  1862) (section 232);

   302                  (l) articles that are entered free of duty as a good of

   313                  Republic, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, or

   315                  Free Trade Agreement.

   317                  15. I find that each exception described in paragraph

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".
query.title: Query

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.
doc_type.title: Doc Type

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).
pres_type.title: Pres Type

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".

    71                  By the authority vested in me as President by the 
    72                  Constitution and the laws of the United States of 
    73                  America, including the International Emergency Economic

    79  
    80                  Section 1. Background. In Executive Order 14193 of 
    81                  February 1, 2025 (Imposing Duties To Address the Flow 
    82                  of Illicit Drugs Across Our Northern Border), I 
    83                  declared a national emergency arising from certain 
    84                  conditions, including the public health crisis caused 
    85                  by fentanyl and other illicit drugs, and the failure of 
    86                  Canada to do more to arrest, seize, detain, or 
    87                  otherwise intercept drug trafficking organizations, 
    88                  other drug or human traffickers, criminals at large, 
    89                  and illicit drugs. In that order, I found that those 
    90                  conditions constitute an unusual and extraordinary 
    91                  threat, which has its source in substantial part 
    92                  outside the United States, to the national security, 
    93                  foreign policy, and economy of the United States.
    94  
    95                  To deal with the emergency declared in Executive Order 
    96                  14193, I imposed an additional ad valorem rate of duty 
    97                  of 25 percent on certain articles that are products of 
    98                  Canada and an additional ad valorem rate of duty of 10 
    99                  percent on certain energy or energy resources that are 
   100                  products of Canada. In Executive Order 14231 of March 
   101                  6, 2025 (Amendment to Duties To Address the Flow of 
   102                  Illicit Drugs Across Our Northern Border), I provided 
   103                  that the additional ad valorem rates of duties under 
   104                  Executive Order 14193 do not apply to articles that are 
   105                  products of Canada that qualify for duty-free entry 
   106                  under the Agreement between the United States of 
   107                  America, United Mexican States, and Canada (USMCA), and 
   108                  I reduced the additional ad valorem rate of duty on 
   109                  potash from 25 percent to 10 percent.
   110  
   111                  Section 2(d) of Executive Order 14193 provides that 
   112                  ``[s]hould Canada retaliate against the United States . 
   113                  . . through import duties on United States exports to 
   114                  Canada or similar measures,'' I ``may increase or 
   115                  expand in scope the duties imposed . . . to ensure the 
   116                  efficacy of th[e] action'' taken in Executive Order 
   117                  14193. Section 3(b) of Executive Order 14193 provides 
   118                  that the Secretary of Homeland Security, in 
   119                  coordination with other senior officials, ``shall 
   120                  recommend additional action, if necessary, should the 
   121                  Government of Canada fail to take adequate steps to 
   122                  alleviate the illegal migration and illicit drug crises 
   123                  through cooperative enforcement actions.''
   124  
   125                  I have received additional information and 
   126                  recommendations from various senior officials 
   127                  regarding, among other things, Canada's lack of 
   128                  cooperation in stemming the flood of fentanyl and other 
   129                  illicit drugs across our northern border--including its 
   130                  failure to devote satisfactory resources to arrest, 
   131                  seize, detain, or otherwise intercept drug trafficking 
   132                  organizations, other drug or human traffickers, 
   133                  criminals at large, and illicit drugs--and Canada's 
   134                  efforts to retaliate against the United States in 
   135                  response to Executive Order 14193, as amended. After 
   136                  considering the additional information and 
   137                  recommendations that I have received, among other 
   138                  things, I have determined that, for the products of 
   139                  Canada that are subject to the additional ad valorem 
   140                  rate of duty of 25 percent, the additional ad valorem 
   141                  rate of duty shall increase from 25 percent to 35 
   142                  percent. In my judgment, this action is
   143  
   144  [[Page 37958]]
   145  
   146                  necessary and appropriate to deal with the emergency 
   147                  declared in Executive Order 14193.
   148  
   149                  Sec. 2. Implementation. (a) All articles that are 
   150                  subject to the additional ad valorem rate of duty of 25 
   151                  percent under Executive Order 14193, as amended, shall 
   152                  instead be subject to an additional ad valorem rate of 
   153                  duty of 35 percent. Accordingly, the Harmonized Tariff 
   154                  Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) shall be modified 
   155                  as provided in the Annex to this order.
   156  
   157                      (b) The changes set forth herein shall be effective 
   158                  with respect to goods entered for consumption, or 
   159                  withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, on or after 
   160                  12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time on August 1, 2025.
   161                      (c) Nothing in this order shall be construed to 
   162                  alter or otherwise affect section 2(b) of Executive 
   163                  Order 14193 or section 2(a) or section 2(b) of 
   164                  Executive Order 14231.
   165                      (d) The stacking rules set out in Executive Order 
   166                  14289 of April 29, 2025 (Addressing Certain Tariffs on 
   167                  Imported Articles), and any subsequent order or 
   168                  proclamation addressing stacking of tariffs imposed 
   169                  under IEEPA, shall continue to apply to goods that are 
   170                  subject to subsection (a) of this section.
   171                      (e) The Secretary of Homeland Security, in 
   172                  consultation with the United States International Trade 
   173                  Commission, shall determine whether any additional 
   174                  modifications to the HTSUS are necessary to effectuate 
   175                  this order and may make such modifications through 
   176                  notice in the Federal Register.
   177  
   178                  Sec. 3. Transshipment. (a) All articles of Canada that 
   179                  do not qualify as originating under USMCA and are 
   180                  determined by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) 
   181                  to have been transshipped to evade applicable duties 
   182                  under section 2 of this order shall be subject to (i) 
   183                  an additional ad valorem rate of duty of 40 percent, in 
   184                  lieu of the additional ad valorem rate of duty 
   185                  applicable under section 2 of this order to goods of 
   186                  the country of origin; (ii) any other applicable or 
   187                  appropriate fine or penalty, including those assessed 
   188                  under 19 U.S.C. 1592; and (iii) any other United States 
   189                  duties, fees, taxes, exactions, or charges applicable 
   190                  to goods of the country of origin. CBP shall not allow, 
   191                  consistent with applicable law, for mitigation or 
   192                  remission of the penalties assessed on imports found to 
   193                  be transshipped to evade applicable duties.
   194  
   195                      (b) The Secretary of Commerce and the Secretary of 
   196                  Homeland Security, acting through the Commissioner of 
   197                  CBP, in consultation with the United States Trade 
   198                  Representative, shall publish every 6 months a list of 
   199                  countries and specific facilities used in circumvention 
   200                  schemes, to inform public procurement, national 
   201                  security reviews, and commercial due diligence.
   202  
   203                  Sec. 4. Monitoring and Recommendations. (a) The 
   204                  Secretary of Homeland Security shall continue to 
   205                  monitor, and regularly consult with the Secretary of 
   206                  State, the Attorney General, the Assistant to the 
   207                  President for National Security Affairs, and the 
   208                  Assistant to the President for Homeland Security, on 
   209                  the situation at our northern border. The Secretary of 
   210                  Homeland Security shall inform the President of any 
   211                  circumstances that, in her opinion, might indicate the 
   212                  need for further action by the President. The Secretary 
   213                  of Homeland Security shall also inform the President of 
   214                  any circumstance that, in her opinion, might indicate 
   215                  that the Government of Canada has taken adequate steps 
   216                  to alleviate the emergency declared in Executive Order 
   217                  14193.
   218  
   219                      (b) The Secretary of Homeland Security, in 
   220                  coordination with the Secretary of State, the Attorney 
   221                  General, the Assistant to the President for National 
   222                  Security Affairs, and the Assistant to the President 
   223                  for Homeland Security, shall recommend additional 
   224                  action, if necessary, should the Government of Canada 
   225                  fail to take adequate steps to alleviate the illicit 
   226                  drug crisis or should the Government of Canada 
   227                  retaliate against the United States in response to the 
   228                  actions taken in Executive Order 14193 or any 
   229                  subsequent order issued to address the emergency 
   230                  declared in Executive Order 14193.
   231  
   232                  Sec. 5. Delegation. The Secretary of Homeland Security, 
   233                  in consultation with the Secretary of the Treasury, the 
   234                  Attorney General, and the Secretary
   235  
   236  [[Page 37959]]
   237  
   238                  of Commerce, is hereby authorized to take such actions, 
   239                  including adopting rules and regulations, and to employ 
   240                  all powers granted to the President by IEEPA as may be 
   241                  necessary to implement this order. The Secretary of 
   242                  Homeland Security may, consistent with applicable law, 
   243                  redelegate any of these functions within the Department 
   244                  of Homeland Security. All executive departments and

   260  
   261  (ii) the functions of the Director of the Office of Management and Budget

    25  Guidance to U.S. Customs and Border Protection Regarding the 
    26  Assessment of ``U.S. Content'' for Purposes of Implementing Tariffs 
    27  Pursuant to Clause (2)(D) of Proclamation 11032 of June 1, 2026
    28  
    29  AGENCY: Bureau of Industry and Security, Department of Commerce.
    30  
    31  ACTION: Notice.
    32  
    33  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    34  
    35  SUMMARY: This notice provides guidance to U.S. Customs and Border 
    36  Protection regarding the assessment of ``U.S. content'' for products of 
    37  Canada and Mexico that qualify for preferential tariff treatment under 
    38  the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, for purposes of implementing 
    39  tariffs pursuant to Proclamation 11032 of June 1, 2026.
    40  
    41  DATES: The guidance set out in in this notice is effective with respect 
    42  to products that are entered for consumption, or withdrawn from 
    43  warehouse for consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. Eastern Time on 
    44  October 14, 2026.
    45  
    46  SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
    47  
    48  Background
    49  
    50      On June 1, 2026, the President issued Presidential Proclamation 
    51  11032 entitled ``Further Adjusting the Tariff Regimes for Imports of 
    52  Aluminum, Steel, and Copper into the United States'' (91 FR 34085) 
    53  (Proclamation). The Proclamation modifies the tariff regimes for metal 
    54  products imposed in Presidential Proclamation 9704, as amended, 
    55  Proclamation 9705, as amended, and Proclamation 10962, as amended, and 
    56  directs the Secretary of Commerce (Secretary) to issue guidance to U.S. 
    57  Customs and Border Protection regarding the assessment of ``U.S. 
    58  content'' for purposes of implementing tariffs pursuant to clause 
    59  (2)(d) of the Proclamation. The Secretary has delegated this duty to 
    60  the Deputy Assistant Secretary for Technology Security.
    61  
    62  Guidance to U.S. Customs and Border Protection Regarding the Assessment 
    63  of ``U.S. Content'' for Purposes of Implementing Tariffs Pursuant to 
    64  Clause (2)(d) of Proclamation 11032 of June 1, 2026
    65  
    66      The Department of Commerce advises that, for purposes of 
    67  implementing clause (2)(d) of the Proclamation, the term ``U.S. 
    68  content'' means the following:
    69      1. The value of the product attributable to parts wholly obtained, 
    70  entirely produced, or substantially transformed in the United States, 
    71  and
    72      2. To the extent not otherwise accounted for in (1), the value of 
    73  the product attributable to steel that was melted and poured in the 
    74  United States, aluminum that was smelted and cast in the United States, 
    75  and/or copper that was smelted and cast in the United States.
    76      Questions regarding the application of this Notice to a specific 
    77  product may be directed to U.S. Customs and Border Protection.
    78  
    79  Jessica Curyto,
    80  Deputy Assistant Secretary for Technology Security.

Document number:   2026-15181
Title:             Notice of Actions in Section 301 Investigations of Acts, Policies, and Practices of Various Economies Related to the Failure of Each Economy To Impose and Effectively Enforce a Prohibition on the Importation of Goods Produced With Forced Labor
Type:              Notice
Action:            Notice of action.
Agencies:          Trade Representative, Office of United States
Citation:          91 FR 47318
Pages:             47318-47662 (345 pages)
Published:         2026-07-28
Dates:             The additional rates of duty are applicable with respect to products that are entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern time on July 24, 2026, except that goods loaded onto a vessel at the port of loading and in transit on the final mode of transit before 12:01 a.m. eastern time on July 24, 2026, and entered for consumption or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption before 12:01 a.m. eastern time on July 28, 2026, shall not be subject to such additional duty.
Docket:            Docket Nos. USTR-2026-0265, USTR-2026-0266
URL:               https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/07/28/2026-15181/notice-of-actions-in-section-301-investigations-of-acts-policies-and-practices-of-various-economies
PDF:               https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-07-28/pdf/2026-15181.pdf

Abstract:
The United States Trade Representative (Trade Representative) has determined under Section 301(b) and Section 304(a) of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (Trade Act), that in each of 60 investigations, certain of the acts, policies, and practices of the economy at issue are actionable and that action by the United States is appropriate. In accordance with the specific direction of the President, the Trade Representative is taking actions in each of these investigations by imposing tariffs on all products of the investigated economy, with certain exemptions as provided in Annexes I and II to this notice (Notice). Consistent with the specific direction of the President, for an economy that imposes a forced labor import prohibition, has committed to impose and enforce such a prohibition through an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (ART), or has imposed a partial regime with the effect of preventing the importation of certain forced labor goods, the Trade Representative has determined 10 percent is the appropriate rate of Section 301 duties, with specific economies subject to a 10 percent rate net of a product's most-favored-nation (MFN) duty. For every other economy, and in accordance with the specific direction of the President, the Trade Representative has determined 12.5 percent is the appropriate rate of Section 301 duty, with specific economies subject to a 12.5 percent rate net of a product's MFN duty. The Trade Representative has also determined, consistent with the specific direction of the President, to establish, when feasible, tariff-rate quotas (TRQs) for Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, and Malaysia, based on each economy's importation of U.S. inputs, to encourage the importation by each of these economies of U.S. cotton and textile goods, in order to reduce reliance on inputs from other sources that are more likely to contain forced labor inputs.

    97  Background
    98  
    99      On February 20, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in Learning 
   100  Resources, Inc. v. Trump that all tariffs imposed by the President 
   101  under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), which 
   102  U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) has collected pursuant to the 
   103  President's Executive Orders and associated provisions in the 
   104  Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) since February 
   105  3, 2025, were unlawful. In so holding, the Supreme Court affirmed the 
   106  August 29, 2025 judgment of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal 
   107  Circuit (CAFC) in V.O.S. Selections, Inc. v. Trump, which in turn had 
   108  affirmed-in-part, vacated-in-part, and remanded-in-part the May 28, 
   109  2025 decision of the U.S. Court of International Trade (CIT) in that 
   110  case. On March 2, 2026, the CAFC issued its formal mandate to the CIT.
   111      On March 4, 2026, the CIT ordered in Atmus Filtration, Inc. v. 
   112  United States ``that, with respect to any and all unliquidated entries 
   113  that were entered subject to the IEEPA duties, U.S. Customs and Border 
   114  Protection is hereby directed to liquidate those entries without regard 
   115  to the IEEPA duties,'' and ``[a]ny liquidated entries for which 
   116  liquidation is not final shall be reliquidated without regard to IEEPA 
   117  duties.'' On March 5, 2026, the CIT amended its March 4, 2026, order in 
   118  Atmus Filtration, Inc. v. United States to clarify that it applies to 
   119  entries made ``subject to the IEEPA duties imposed by the Executive 
   120  Orders considered by the Supreme Court in Learning Resources, Inc. v. 
   121  Trump.'' On March 6, 2026, the CIT suspended its March 4, 2026, order, 
   122  as amended, ``to the extent that it directs immediate compliance,'' to 
   123  allow CBP time to develop an automated tool capable of processing the 
   124  unprecedented volume and value of refunds covered by the CIT order. On 
   125  the same day, the CIT also ordered the government to provide periodic 
   126  status reporting on this development. The government submitted detailed 
   127  status reports to the court on March 12, 2026, and March 19, 2026.
   128      On March 20, 2026, the CIT again amended its Amended Order of March 
   129  5, 2026, to clarify that it applies to ``any and all unliquidated 
   130  entries that were entered subject to IEEPA duties'' as well as to any 
   131  such ``liquidated entries for which liquidation is not final,'' 
   132  provided, however, that ``nothing in this order addresses issues 
   133  concerning duty free de minimis treatment under 19 U.S.C. 1321 that are 
   134  otherwise before this Court'' in Axle of Dearborn, Inc. v. Department 
   135  of Commerce. The CIT's March 20, 2026 order continued to suspend the 
   136  Amended Order of March 5, 2026, ``to the extent that it requires 
   137  immediate compliance,'' and ordered that the government file another 
   138  status report on March 31, 2026, ``describing the progress Customs has 
   139  made toward the completion of a process to issue refunds of IEEPA 
   140  duties paid with interest,'' and join another closed settlement 
   141  conference with the Court later the same day to further discuss the 
   142  same. In accordance with this order, the government submitted a 
   143  detailed status report and attended a closed settlement conference on 
   144  March 31, 2026. On April 6, 2026, the plaintiff in Atmus Filtration, 
   145  Inc. v. United States filed a notice of voluntary dismissal in its 
   146  case, which the CIT granted on April 8, 2026.
   147      On April 7, 2026, the CIT lifted the stay on Euro-Notions Florida, 
   148  Inc. v. United States, CIT Ct. No. 25-00595, another pending case 
   149  challenging the IEEPA duties, and issued an injunctive order 
   150  substantively identical to its March 4, 2026, order, as amended, in 
   151  Atmus Filtration, Inc. Accordingly, the Euro-Notions Florida, Inc. case 
   152  has replaced the Atmus Filtration, Inc. case as the test case for the 
   153  IEEPA refund process. On April 8, 2026, the CIT issued an order in 
   154  Euro-Notions Florida, Inc. ordering the government to file another 
   155  status update on April 14, 2026, regarding CBP's progress on the IEEPA 
   156  duty refund process and join another closed settlement conference with 
   157  the Court later the same day.
   158      Specifically, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and CBP 
   159  have initiated the development of the Consolidated Administration and 
   160  Processing of Entries (CAPE) tool to handle the volume of tariff 
   161  refunds anticipated in the timeframe required by the CIT. While the CIT 
   162  has not set a timeframe to date, the Court has signaled that refunds be 
   163  issued as quickly as possible because of the accrual of interest. 
   164  Further, while the order to refund IEEPA duties with interest is 
   165  currently suspended ``to the extent that it requires immediate 
   166  compliance,'' the CIT is closely monitoring CBP's progress to timely 
   167  complete the development of CAPE and can lift the suspension of its 
   168  order at any time.
   169      The tariffs assessed under IEEPA from February 3, 2025 to February 
   170  24, 2026 total an estimated $166 billion, with over 53 million entry 
   171  summaries requiring processing in order to issue accurate refunds with 
   172  required interest. Prior to CAPE, refunds were reviewed and processed 
   173  entry summary-by-entry summary. Given the volume and values of the 
   174  entries affected by the CIT order, CBP is unable to process the refunds 
   175  owed in a timely or efficient manner using the existing process.
   176      The CAPE tool may be accessed through CBP's Automated Commercial 
   177  Environment (ACE), which is the CBP-operated system used to report, 
   178  manage, process, and track U.S. imports and exports.
   179      The CAPE tool allows CBP to process multiple entry summaries by the 
   180  same importer on a single submission, which will lead to a single 
   181  refund for a given importer rather than multiple refund transactions. 
   182  Importers are able to file as many CAPE Declarations as they need. 
   183  Thus, potentially thousands of refund transactions can be consolidated 
   184  into a single payment that is directly deposited into an IOR's account 
   185  (or the account of their designated party) on file. The request for a 
   186  refund that is filed through CAPE is called a ``CAPE Declaration''.
   187      The new CAPE tool allows--
   188       Automated processes to be leveraged to the fullest extent 
   189  possible to segment risk and execute millions of mathematical 
   190  calculations with precision.
   191       CBP personnel to focus on those refund CAPE Declarations 
   192  that are considered ``high risk'' due to the dollar values involved or 
   193  the risk profile of the IOR.
   194       CBP personnel to determine with confidence which lines on 
   195  an entry summary are eligible for an IEEPA refund while ensuring the 
   196  remaining duties (including duties owed for antidumping/countervailing 
   197  duty (AD/CVD) remedies and Section 232 tariffs), tax, and fees that are 
   198  owed the U.S. government are retained and collected as usual.
   199       CBP personnel to ensure that the precise duty owed to the 
   200  IOR is refunded directly to the IOR's account--
   201  
   202  [[Page 63301]]
   203  
   204  no overpayments or payments to an erroneous party.
   205      IORs will submit the information related to their refund request to 
   206  CBP through the ACE Portal. Alternatively, IORs may have their 
   207  information submitted to CBP using a licensed customs broker. Brokers 
   208  are licensed through CBP to conduct customs business on behalf of their 
   209  IOR clients. In order to receive a refund through the CAPE process, the 
   210  IOR, or their designated broker, must have an active and up-to-date ACE 
   211  Portal account and supporting profile. If a broker is filing a CAPE 
   212  Declaration on an IOR's behalf, they must be the ``notify party'' 
   213  designated in the appropriate ACE account. Only ACE account holders 
   214  will be able to file a CAPE Declaration through the CAPE tool.
   215      Most small businesses do not have an ACE account and instead enlist 
   216  the assistance of a licensed customs broker to conduct business on 
   217  their behalf. They will continue to be able, and are expected, to use 
   218  their customs brokers for the IEEPA refunds process and CAPE.
   219      It is also important to note that the Federal Government no longer 
   220  disburses paper checks, but issues refunds electronically via Automated 
   221  Clearinghouse (ACH). The transition to electronic refunds is in line 
   222  with Executive Order 12247 and was implemented by CBP via the Interim 
   223  Final Rule (IFR) Electronic Refunds (91 FR 21) in January 2026. CBP is 
   224  currently holding refunds for filers who do not have an ACH account on 
   225  file in ACE. CBP will continue to do the same for IEEPA Refunds. As 
   226  noted in the IFR: ``If an importer believes that one of the waiver 
   227  criteria in 31 CFR part 208 applies and seeks payment of its refund via 
   228  a U.S. Treasury check, the importer must notify CBP's Revenue Division 
   229  in writing at [email protected].'' CBP does not believe 
   230  it is necessary at this time to create a procedure outside the one 
   231  established in the IFR.
   232      The term ``Declaration filer'' will be used going forward to cover 
   233  both IORs who file their own IEEPA refund requests or their designated 
   234  licensed customs broker.
   235

   237

   239  submitted to OMB for consideration of approval on an emergency 
   240  clearance, with the justification of an unanticipated event and reasons 
   241  to believe following the normal PRA process is likely to prevent or 
   242  disrupt the collection of information and cause public harm. CBP 
   243  welcomes public to comment on these approved changes.
   244      To submit an IEEPA refund CAPE declaration, an IOR, or their 
   245  broker, will submit a Comma-Separated Values (CSV) file with a list of

   247  Depending on the CAPE Declaration, this file may contain only a few

   250                  reciprocal treatment to U.S. exports in the context of 
   251                  bilateral trade negotiations.
   252  
   253                  These structural asymmetries have driven the large and 
   254                  persistent annual U.S. goods trade deficit. Even for 
   255                  countries with which the United States may enjoy an 
   256                  occasional bilateral trade surplus, the accumulation of 
   257                  tariff and non-tariff barriers on U.S. exports may make 
   258                  that surplus smaller than it would have been without 
   259                  such barriers. Permitting these asymmetries to continue 
   260                  is not sustainable in today's economic and geopolitical 
   261                  environment because of the effect they have on U.S. 
   262                  domestic production. A nation's ability to produce 
   263                  domestically is the bedrock of its national and 
   264                  economic security.
   265  
   266                  Both my first Administration in 2017, and the Biden 
   267                  Administration in 2022, recognized that increasing 
   268                  domestic manufacturing is critical to U.S. national 
   269                  security. According to 2023 United Nations data, U.S. 
   270                  manufacturing output as a share of global manufacturing 
   271                  output was 17.4 percent, down from a peak in 2001 of 
   272                  28.4 percent.
   273  
   274                  Over time, the persistent decline in U.S. manufacturing 
   275                  output has reduced U.S. manufacturing capacity. The 
   276                  need to maintain robust and resilient domestic 
   277                  manufacturing capacity is particularly acute in certain 
   278                  advanced industrial sectors like automobiles, 
   279                  shipbuilding, pharmaceuticals, technology products, 
   280                  machine tools, and basic and fabricated metals, because 
   281                  once competitors gain sufficient global market share in 
   282                  these sectors, U.S. production could be permanently 
   283                  weakened. It is also critical to scale manufacturing 
   284                  capacity in the defense-industrial sector so that we 
   285                  can manufacture the defense materiel and equipment 
   286                  necessary to protect American interests at home and 
   287                  abroad.
   288  
   289                  In fact, because the United States has supplied so much 
   290                  military equipment to other countries, U.S. stockpiles 
   291                  of military goods are too low to be compatible with 
   292                  U.S. national defense interests. Furthermore, U.S. 
   293                  defense companies must develop new, advanced 
   294                  manufacturing technologies across a range of critical 
   295                  sectors including bio-manufacturing, batteries, and 
   296                  microelectronics. If the United States wishes to 
   297                  maintain an effective security umbrella to defend its 
   298                  citizens and homeland, as well as for its allies and 
   299                  partners, it needs to have a large upstream 
   300                  manufacturing and goods-producing ecosystem to 
   301                  manufacture these products without undue reliance on 
   302                  imports for key inputs.
   303  
   304                  Increased reliance on foreign producers for goods also 
   305                  has compromised U.S. economic security by rendering 
   306                  U.S. supply chains vulnerable to geopolitical 
   307                  disruption and supply shocks. In recent years, the 
   308                  vulnerability of the U.S. economy in this respect was 
   309                  exposed both during the COVID-19 pandemic, when 
   310                  Americans had difficulty accessing essential products, 
   311                  as well as when the Houthi rebels later began attacking 
   312                  cargo ships in the Middle East.
   313  
   314                  The decline of U.S. manufacturing capacity threatens 
   315                  the U.S. economy in other ways, including through the 
   316                  loss of manufacturing jobs. From 1997 to 2024, the 
   317                  United States lost around 5 million manufacturing jobs 
   318                  and experienced one of the largest drops in 
   319                  manufacturing employment in history. Furthermore, many 
   320                  manufacturing job losses were concentrated in specific 
   321                  geographical areas. In these areas, the loss of 
   322                  manufacturing jobs contributed
   323  
   324  [[Page 15044]]
   325  
   326                  to the decline in rates of family formation and to the 
   327                  rise of other social trends, like the abuse of opioids, 
   328                  that have imposed profound costs on the U.S. economy.
   329  
   330                  The future of American competitiveness depends on 
   331                  reversing these trends. Today, manufacturing represents 
   332                  just 11 percent of U.S. gross domestic product, yet it 
   333                  accounts for 35 percent of American productivity growth 
   334                  and 60 percent of our exports. Importantly, U.S. 
   335                  manufacturing is the main engine of innovation in the 
   336                  United States, responsible for 55 percent of all 
   337                  patents and 70 percent of all research and development 
   338                  (R&D) spending. The fact that R&D expenditures by U.S. 
   339                  multinational enterprises in China grew at an average 
   340                  rate of 13.6 percent a year between 2003 and 2017, 
   341                  while their R&D expenditures in the United States grew 
   342                  by an average of just 5 percent per year during the 
   343                  same time period, is evidence of the strong link 
   344                  between manufacturing and innovation. Furthermore, 
   345                  every manufacturing job spurs 7 to 12 new jobs in other 
   346                  related industries, helping to build and sustain our 
   347                  economy.
   348  
   349                  Just as a nation that does not produce manufactured 
   350                  products cannot maintain the industrial base it needs 
   351                  for national security, neither can a nation long 
   352                  survive if it cannot produce its own food. Presidential 
   353                  Policy Directive 21 of February 12, 2013 (Critical 
   354                  Infrastructure Security and Resilience), designates 
   355                  food and agriculture as a ``critical infrastructure 
   356                  sector'' because it is one of the sectors considered 
   357                  ``so vital to the United States that [its] incapacity 
   358                  or destruction . . . would have a debilitating impact 
   359                  on security, national economic security, national 
   360                  public health or safety, or any combination of those 
   361                  matters.'' Furthermore, when I left office, the United 
   362                  States had a trade surplus in agricultural products, 
   363                  but today, that surplus has vanished. Eviscerated by a 
   364                  slew of new non-tariff barriers imposed by our trading 
   365                  partners, it has been replaced by a projected $49 
   366                  billion annual agricultural trade deficit.
   367  
   368                  For these reasons, I hereby declare and order:
   369  
   370                  Section 1. National Emergency. As President of the 
   371                  United States, my highest duty is ensuring the national 
   372                  and economic security of the country and its citizens.
   373  
   374                  I have declared a national emergency arising from 
   375                  conditions reflected in large and persistent annual 
   376                  U.S. goods trade deficits, which have grown by over 40 
   377                  percent in the past 5 years alone, reaching $1.2 
   378                  trillion in 2024. This trade deficit reflects 
   379                  asymmetries in trade relationships that have 
   380                  contributed to the atrophy of domestic production 
   381                  capacity, especially that of the U.S. manufacturing and 
   382                  defense-industrial base. These asymmetries also impact 
   383                  U.S. producers' ability to export and, consequentially, 
   384                  their incentive to produce.
   385  
   386                  Specifically, such asymmetry includes not only non-
   387                  reciprocal differences in tariff rates among foreign 
   388                  trading partners, but also extensive use of non-tariff 
   389                  barriers by foreign trading partners, which reduce the 
   390                  competitiveness of U.S. exports while artificially 
   391                  enhancing the competitiveness of their own goods. These 
   392                  non-tariff barriers include technical barriers to 
   393                  trade; non-scientific sanitary and phytosanitary rules; 
   394                  inadequate intellectual property protections; 
   395                  suppressed domestic consumption (e.g., wage 
   396                  suppression); weak labor, environmental, and other 
   397                  regulatory standards and protections; and corruption. 
   398                  These non-tariff barriers give rise to significant 
   399                  imbalances even when the United States and a trading 
   400                  partner have comparable tariff rates.
   401  
   402                  The cumulative effect of these imbalances has been the 
   403                  transfer of resources from domestic producers to 
   404                  foreign firms, reducing opportunities for domestic 
   405                  manufacturers to expand and, in turn, leading to lost 
   406                  manufacturing jobs, diminished manufacturing capacity, 
   407                  and an atrophied industrial base, including in the 
   408                  defense-industrial sector. At the same time, foreign 
   409                  firms are better positioned to scale production, 
   410                  reinvest in innovation, and compete
   411  
   412  [[Page 15045]]
   413  
   414                  in the global economy, to the detriment of U.S. 
   415                  economic and national security.
   416  
   417                  The absence of sufficient domestic manufacturing 
   418                  capacity in certain critical and advanced industrial 
   419                  sectors--another outcome of the large and persistent 
   420                  annual U.S. goods trade deficits--also compromises U.S. 
   421                  economic and national security by rendering the U.S. 
   422                  economy less resilient to supply chain disruption. 
   423                  Finally, the large, persistent annual U.S. goods trade 
   424                  deficits, and the concomitant loss of industrial

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".
query.title: Query

doc_type.description: Document types: RULE, PRORULE (proposed rule), NOTICE, PRESDOCU (presidential document). null for all.
doc_type.title: Doc Type

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).
pres_type.title: Pres Type

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

**Considering product scope**

I'm noticing that there's some concern about the product list and its effective date of October 338. It seems there are no other images involved in this. The September scope indicates that stacking applies to all products, which should clear up any ambiguity. I want to make sure that this is understood clearly to avoid any confusion going forward. Let's keep all these factors in mind!
